verses.1: Al-Mizan reads (83:1) and (83:2-3) as a curse on taṭfīf, giving short count or weight, which God prohibits as ifsād, corruption on earth (11:85). It distinguishes iktiyāl, receiving by measure, from kayl, giving by measure; receiving one’s right fully (istīfāʾ) while inflicting loss (ikhsār) when giving is the stated injustice. The criticism is that defrauders acknowledge their own rights but not others’, undermining the reciprocal rights and duties on which a just society rests. Suggested explanations for 83:2 mentioning measure but not weight—wholesale merchants and taghlīb, or weight being implicit—are judged incompatible with (83:3); the claim that the audience bought only by measure but sold by both measure and weight lacks evidence. Other explanations are likewise not persuasive.

verses.4: Al-Mizan takes the question as a surprised negation: the defrauders do not even suppose that they, marked as ulāʾika to indicate remoteness from God’s mercy, will be raised on the tremendous Day of Resurrection and repaid for their deeds. It gives ẓann its usual sense of supposition, despite a reported reading of it as knowledge. Although certainty about the hereafter is obligatory, even its possibility should deter this grave sin: people take precautions against anticipated loss even without certainty, and possible accountability and severe punishment demand restraint. Standing before the Lord means rising from graves and awaiting His judgment.

verses.7: Al-Mizan says kallā dismisses the defrauders’ practice and their heedlessness of resurrection and reckoning. Contrasted with ʿIlliyyūn, ‘the highest of the high,’ Sijjīn conveys abasement and confinement and is best read as an intensive form of sijn, prison: a place confining its occupant for a long time or forever. Kitāb means maktūb, what is written, from kitābah in the sense of a definite decree. Thus the vicious have a divinely decreed retribution in Sijjīn, a prison from which they do not escape.
verses.8: Al-Mizan takes ‘What will show you what Sijjīn is?’ as an expression of intense terror; an editor notes that Sijjīn may be rendered ‘the Lowest Hell’ or ‘the Infernal Record.’
verses.9: Al-Mizan treats the written record as explaining Sijjīn. Here kitāb is maktūb, decreed and recorded by kitābah, and raqm is most suitably a marked inscription that makes the decree unambiguous and irrevocable. Sijjīn is therefore clearly decreed as the vicious’ eternal abode; the record is in Sijjīn because Sijjīn is the broader record containing the fates of all who merit punishment, not only the vicious. An editor instead says the repeated kitāb more fluently refers back to 83:7: it is inscribed unequivocally that the vicious are destined for Sijjīn; on that reading, ‘What will show you?’ is itself a complete intensifier and need not require the following verse to define Sijjīn.
verses.10: Al-Mizan connects (83:7), 83:8, (83:9), and (83:10) as one thread: the vicious are deniers, cursed because on that Day their decreed punishment in Sijjīn will occur. It reports, then declines to analyse separately, readings that take kitāb as the sinners’ deed-record or its inscription; make Sijjīn the lowest earth, a valley or well of hell, the name of a record, a place for records, an all-evil register, total humiliation, or a form of sijjīl; distinguish its two occurrences as place and record; make 83:7-9 parenthetical; or make (83:9) explain the kitāb of (83:7) rather than Sijjīn. It judges such proposals unsupported and disruptive of the parallel with 83:18-21. The deniers of Retribution are apparently outspoken disbelievers, so the rebuke principally concerns faithless defrauders rather than sinful believers; yet denial may possibly include denial in practice, extending it to all wrongdoers. Athīm and muʿtadī denote accumulated sin and transgression beyond servitude: habitual desire and sin make restraint unwelcome and can culminate in outright denial of resurrection and reckoning (30:10).

verses.13: Al-Mizan infers from ‘recited’ that God’s signs are Qur’anic verses. Asāṭīr, writings in lines, here means the superstitious legends of ancient peoples: when warned through the Qur’an against disobedience, resurrection, and retribution, the deniers dismiss it as meaningless tales.
verses.14: Al-Mizan says kallā rejects the deniers’ claim that the Qur’an is ancient fables. Their sins are what have sullied their hearts: rayn is rust or stain over a polished surface, so evil deeds veil the heart from truth and from distinguishing good from evil. Such deeds leave forms and impressions on the soul that obstruct perception. By contrast, the soul in its pristine state is pure, transparent, and polished, able to know truth from falsehood and virtue from vice (91:7-8).
verses.15: Al-Mizan takes kallā to refute the sins that have blocked the deniers’ hearts. Their alienation from their Lord on the Day of Resurrection is deprivation of an honourable nearness to Him, perhaps what some exegetes call being veiled from His mercy. It does not mean that they will lack all knowledge of Him: then all intermediate causes fall away and everyone knows the Lord, as (40:16) and (24:25) indicate.
verses.16: Al-Mizan reads thumma in (83:16) and (83:17) as marking distinct clauses, not a temporal interval. It reports two readings: the deniers will enter hell and remain there, or will enter it and feel its heat. ‘This is what you used to deny’ is a reproach, spoken either by hell’s keepers or by the people of paradise.

verses.18: Al-Mizan reads (83:18-20) in parallel with (83:7-9). ʿIlliyyūn, ‘elevation above elevation,’ signifies lofty stations of nearness to God, opposed to Sijjīn; the virtuous’ recompense is written and decreed there with inevitable clarity. It reports but rejects as unsupported the suggestions that it is the seventh heaven beneath the Throne, the Lote Tree, a jeweled tablet beneath the Throne, or ranks clothed in divine majesty. The muqarrabūn are not testifying but observing that record or ʿIlliyyūn; they are the superior subset of paradise’s inhabitants, the people of certitude, as their drinking from its spring in (83:28) confirms. The alternatives that they are angels present with deed-records, or angels together with the virtuous, depend on the rejected reading of kitāb as a deed-record.

verses.22: Al-Mizan defines naʿīm as abundant blessing, whose indefiniteness magnifies bliss beyond description. Arāʾik are beds in bridal chambers. Since the object of the virtuous’ looking is left unspecified, it most plausibly means the refreshing scenes and enduring bounties of paradise, not the punishment of disbelievers, as some propose.

verses.24: Al-Mizan defines naḍrah as radiance and freshness. Though the address is to the Prophet because he may observe it, its force is general: anyone looking at the virtuous’ faces will recognize the freshness and happiness of their bliss.
verses.25: Al-Mizan defines raḥīq as wine pure and unadulterated. Its being sealed suits its preciousness, since sealing preserves it from contaminating mixture or impurity.
verses.26: Al-Mizan reports two senses of khitām: the wine is sealed with musk rather than worldly clay, or its final taste and aroma are musk. Tanāfus is rivalry in acquiring a prize, here competition or racing, so the verse urges striving for the sealed distilled wine (83:25), as other calls urge racing toward forgiveness (57:21) and good works (5:48). A note observes a grammatical difficulty in placing ‘for such’ before the command. Reported answers either posit an omitted condition—if anyone competes, let them compete for this—or make the verse encourage both paradise’s bounties generally and this particular wine specifically.
verses.27: Al-Mizan defines mizāj as the means of blending and Tasnīm as a fountain in paradise, whose root conveys elevation and fullness. It reports that shariba may occur with or without bi, and that ʿaynan may be accusative through an implied ‘I praise’ or ‘I mean.’ The near ones, al-muqarrabūn, drink Tasnīm pure and entire, while the virtuous, al-abrār, receive it as a seasoning in their wine; Tasnīm is therefore the higher drink and its drinkers rank above the main group described here. An editor adds that bi can mark direct contact: the near ones have direct access at the highest level of paradise, while the virtuous receive its mixture further down.

verses.29: Al-Mizan identifies the faithful with the virtuous of (83:22), called faithful because their faith occasioned the mockery, and calls the mockers guilty because they derided believers. The guilty laughed, exchanged contemptuous winks when passing them, and returned home either exulting boastfully or chatting humorously about their conduct. When they called the believers astray, they presumptuously assumed the role of witnesses or, more apparently, judges.

verses.33: Al-Mizan treats (83:33) as a condemnation of the mockers: they were not appointed guardians over believers, entitled to judge them or testify against them as they pleased.
verses.34: Al-Mizan makes ‘today’ the Day of Judgment. The unusual preposing of ‘the faithless’ signals a reversal: those who laughed at the faithful in this world will now be laughed at by them. The faithful’s reclining on couches and observing are further predicates of their state.

verses.36: Al-Mizan gives thawāb its broad sense of payment or compensation, though it commonly denotes reward. The believers’ observation from couches in bridal chambers is the faithless’ recompense for laughing at believers, winking disdainfully at them, returning home exultant, and pronouncing them astray.
